werk/beyonce-the-lion-king-the-gift.text:
This album accompanies the 2019 Disney remake of The Lion King. Beyoncé produced and compiled it. She herself called it sonic cinema: new songs, inspired by the story of the film. Because the film is set in Africa, she worked with African producers and artists, including Wizkid, Burna Boy and Tiwa Savage. Between the songs are short interludes that follow the storyline.

The music mixes R&B, pop, hip hop, gqom and afrobeats. Brown Skin Girl won an award at the Soul Train Music Awards. Critics were mostly positive. AllMusic spoke of an Afro-pop hybrid, and The Guardian wrote that the album gave afrobeats a large new audience. Several reviewers felt that the record works best if you forget the film.
werk/beyonce-the-lion-king-the-gift.listen: Listen to Brown Skin Girl and notice how well the song stands on its own, even without the film.

werk/big-star-1-record.text:
As fifteen-year-olds, Alex Chilton and Chris Bell saw the Beatles in 1966 in their home town of Memphis. That remained their example: they wanted to write like Lennon and McCartney and put the name Bell/Chilton on as many songs as possible. The album was released on Ardent Records in Memphis. Many tracks grew in the studio: Chilton brought something raw, Bell added sweet backing vocals. Bell, the technical driving force behind the recordings, was an official member only on this album, and producer John Fry finished the mix with great care.

The sound is more polished than on the later albums. There are harmonies, rock songs and acoustic ballads, such as Thirteen and Watch the Sunrise. Reviews were glowing, but the album was poorly distributed and sold fewer than ten thousand copies. Interest only grew in the late 1970s, when EMI reissued it in England together with Radio City. It is now regarded as a foundational work of power pop.
werk/big-star-1-record.listen: Listen to Thirteen and notice the quiet acoustic accompaniment and how tender and simple the vocal sounds.

werk/big-star-radio-city.text:
In late 1972, after the debut #1 Record, founder Chris Bell left the group and the band lay idle for four months. Alex Chilton then finished part of the recordings with drummer Richard Rosebrough and sometimes bassist Danny Jones. After a performance at the Rock Writers Convention in 1973, the band went back into the studio. Radio City was recorded in late 1973 at Ardent Studios in Memphis. Bell had co-written O My Soul and Back of a Car, but was not on the credits.

The record came out in February 1974 and was praised by critics. Even so, sales stalled at about 20,000 copies, because distribution ground to a halt through a quarrel between Stax and Columbia. September Gurls and Back of a Car are among the band's best-known songs. Over the years its reputation grew, and the record is now regarded as a milestone of power pop.
werk/big-star-radio-city.listen: Listen to September Gurls and notice how the song is catchy and yet sounds slightly askew, exactly the combination critics wrote about.

werk/big-youth-hit-the-road-jack.text:
Hit the Road Jack was released in 1976 and is a reggae album by Manley Buchanan of Kingston, Jamaica, better known as Big Youth. The record was made at Randy's in Kingston, with Karl Pitterson and Errol Thompson as engineers. The album consists of ten tracks on which only Big Youth himself is credited as a vocalist.

The choice of well-known songs by others is striking. Buchanan gives a reggae version of What's Going On by Marvin Gaye, of Hit the Road Jack by Percy Mayfield and of Wake Up Everybody, the song by Victor Carstarphen, Gene McFadden and John Whitehead. Get Up, Stand Up by Bob Marley and Peter Tosh is also on the record. The remaining tracks he wrote himself. In 2011 he discussed his version of Hit the Road Jack in an interview for the BBC series Reggae Britannia.
werk/big-youth-hit-the-road-jack.listen: Listen to Hit the Road Jack and compare it with the original you may know: what changes in the rhythm and in the way the voice delivers the lyrics?

werk/bill-evans-empathy.text:
Pianist Bill Evans and drummer Shelly Manne were playing together on the programme at the Village Vanguard in New York when Verve producer Creed Taylor proposed a studio session. Riverside, the label to which Evans was then tied, gave permission. Manne brought his bassist Monty Budwig, so that a trio came about. Evans moved to Verve a year later.

The record features well-known standards alongside two songs by Irving Berlin from the musical Mr. President. The attention is mainly on Evans, but the critic Leonard Feather observed that the interplay with Manne lifts the music far above that of an ordinary piano trio. A reviewer at AllMusic hears an Evans who plays more lightly, freely and relaxedly than before, as if the three musicians were enjoying a day away from their regular groups.
werk/bill-evans-empathy.listen: In With a Song in My Heart, the longest track, listen to how piano, bass and drums play together.

werk/bill-evans-new-jazz-conceptions.text:
Bill Evans made his debut as a leader in September 1956 for Riverside. The guitarist Mundell Lowe had played a demo tape of Evans to the producer Orrin Keepnews. Keepnews and Bill Grauer then heard him several times at the Village Vanguard and offered him a contract. Evans had to be persuaded to record.

The record contains eight trio recordings with bassist Teddy Kotick and drummer Paul Motian, interspersed with three very short piano solos: I Got It Bad, My Romance and the first version of Waltz for Debby. Three of Evans's own pieces are also included, among them Five, which Evans went on playing throughout his career. Reviews were good, but only 800 copies were sold in the first year. Evans then did not record a record of his own for more than two years.
werk/bill-evans-new-jazz-conceptions.listen: Listen to Waltz for Debby, which lasts a little over a minute: this is the first recording of a melody that Evans would often play again later.

werk/bill-evans-undercurrent.text:
After the death of the bassist Scott LaFaro in July 1961, the pianist Bill Evans recorded nothing for months and did not even play. When he began again in October, it was as an accompanist for others. Only with this album, recorded in the spring of 1962, was he a bandleader again. His partner was the guitarist Jim Hall. The duo knew each other from the circle around George Russell.

The programme consists of standards and pieces by others, with no original pieces by Evans. My Funny Valentine is a brisk number here, whereas it is usually a heavy-hearted ballad. Evans and Hall both play chordal instruments, but they avoid things getting too busy, because they leave a great deal of space and every note counts. The DownBeat reviewer called it one of the most beautiful records he had ever heard. The sleeve shows a photograph by Toni Frissell.
werk/bill-evans-undercurrent.listen: Listen to My Funny Valentine and notice how piano and guitar give each other room at the fast tempo.

werk/bill-haley-en-his-comets-rock-n-rol.text:
This album was released in August 1956 on Decca and was the band's first with new material rather than previously released tracks. Bill Haley and His Comets were not featured on it only for their singer: Haley can be heard on just four tracks. The other band members were given room.

Saxophonist Rudy Pompilli plays the lead in the instrumental Rudy's Rock, guitarist Franny Beecher in Goofin' Around and Blue Comet Blues, and steel guitarist Billy Williamson sings Hide and Seek by Big Joe Turner. On Rockin' Thru the Rye, Haley turned a poem by Robert Burns into a rock 'n' roll song. Almost all the tracks were new and written by Haley or his Comets. Some of them were heard in the film Don't Knock the Rock. In England the album spent a week at number one in 1956.
werk/bill-haley-en-his-comets-rock-n-rol.listen: Listen to Rudy's Rock and notice how Rudy Pompilli's tenor saxophone takes the place of the singer.

werk/bill-withers-just-as-i-am.text:
This debut was released on 1 May 1971 on Sussex Records. Booker T. Jones produced the record, arranged the songs and played keyboards and guitar. On the sleeve Bill Withers stands next to a brick building, in a yellow T-shirt and carrying a lunch box, at what is reportedly the factory where he was then working, installing toilets for aircraft.

The album contains Ain't No Sunshine, which Rolling Stone later placed at number 280 on its list of the 500 greatest songs of all time, and Grandma's Hands, which reached eighteenth place on the soul chart. Robert Christgau wrote that Withers is more folk than pop and that he combines gospel fire with folk seriousness, which makes titles such as I'm Her Daddy and Better Off Dead sound like radical protest. In 2020 Rolling Stone placed the record at number 304 of the 500 greatest albums.
werk/bill-withers-just-as-i-am.listen: Listen to Ain't No Sunshine and notice his voice, which according to one reviewer sounds more folk than pop.

werk/bill-withers-justments.text:
Bill Withers's third album was released on 6 April 1974 on Sussex Records. On the sleeve he writes himself why the record has that title: life gives us the responsibility of furnishing our own psyche, we make mistakes and then have to adjust, what the old people back home called justments. Withers produced the record together with the bassist Melvin Dunlap and the drummer James Gadson.

The single The Same Love That Made Me Laugh reached fiftieth place in the United States in the spring of 1974. José Feliciano plays guitar on Can We Pretend and congas on Railroad Man. Withers had earlier contributed to Compartments, a 1973 album by Feliciano. Legal disputes with Sussex then prevented new recording sessions, until Columbia signed him a year later. The record itself only came out on CD in 2010.
werk/bill-withers-justments.listen: Listen to Railroad Man and try to pick out José Feliciano's congas.

werk/bill-withers-still-bill.text:
Still Bill is Bill Withers's second studio album and was released on 1 May 1972 on Sussex Records. Withers recorded and produced it himself, with musicians from the Watts 103rd Street Rhythm Band. His first album was Just as I Am. The music mixes soul, funk and blues, and the lyrics deal with human nature, emotions and sex, seen from a male middle-class perspective.

The album contains two of his best-known songs. Lean on Me became number 1 on both the pop chart and the R&B chart of Billboard, and Use Me reached number 2. By September 1972 the album had already gone gold. Reviews were positive: Rolling Stone found it stronger and more relaxed than his debut, and later critics called it a classic of the 1970s. The production is sparse, with in Use Me a famous guitar motif by Ray Jackson.
werk/bill-withers-still-bill.listen: Listen to Use Me and notice the catchy motif that carries the song, and how sober the rest of the accompaniment is.

werk/billie-eilish-happier-than-ever.text:
Billie Eilish wrote the album with her brother Finneas O'Connell, who also produced it and played all the instruments. They recorded it between April 2020 and February 2021 in his home studio in the basement of his house in Los Angeles, beginning with my future and ending with Oxytocin. Self-reflection during the coronavirus pandemic was her greatest inspiration. She said that almost no song is cheerful, despite the title.

It sounds calmer than the debut: downtempo pop with sober, jazzy electropop arrangements, acoustic guitars and soft synthesizers. The lyrics deal with the downside of fame, abuse and mistrust. Getting Older opens the album, Your Power is a gentle acoustic ballad. The album received glowing reviews and seven Grammy nominations, including Album of the Year, and reached number 1 in the United States.
werk/billie-eilish-happier-than-ever.listen: Listen to Happier Than Ever and notice how the song begins as a soft, sad break-up song and bursts into an ending driven by electric guitar.

werk/billie-eilish-when-we-all-fall-asle.text:
This debut album was released on 29 March 2019, when Billie Eilish was seventeen. She wrote it largely with her brother Finneas O'Connell, who produced it in his small bedroom studio in Highland Park, Los Angeles. They chose that room for its homely atmosphere and because a studio was expensive and had little daylight. The title comes from a line in Bury a Friend. Lucid dreams and nightmares were part of the inspiration for the album.

It sounds like electropop and art pop, with influences from hip hop and industrial. The production centres on amplified bass, minimal percussion and extra sounds. The lyrics deal with youth today, addiction, heartbreak and mental health, with humour and horror. Bad Guy became a worldwide hit. The album received glowing reviews and in 2020 won the Grammy for Album of the Year, alongside three other major Grammys for Eilish and Finneas.
werk/billie-eilish-when-we-all-fall-asle.listen: Listen to bad guy and notice the minimal percussion and the heavy bass beneath the soft, almost whispered vocals.

werk/billie-holiday-lady-in-satin.text:
After twelve albums with small jazz combos for Norman Granz, Billie Holiday moved to Columbia in 1957. She wanted a beautiful, tender album with an orchestra as a cushion beneath her voice, not a wild jam session. Producer Irving Townsend arranged the recordings in February 1958 with the arranger Ray Ellis, who used an orchestra of forty, with strings, brass, reeds and a small choir. It became her most expensive production.

The songs come from the Great American Songbook. After years of drink and drugs her voice had become fragile and hoarse, but her own phrasing and the sharp edge had remained. The reactions were mixed. The Penguin Guide to Jazz spoke of a voyeuristic look at a broken woman, whereas the trumpeter Buck Clayton actually preferred the later singer to the younger one. Ellis remembered her tears on listening back to I'm a Fool to Want You. In 2000 the album entered the Grammy Hall of Fame.
werk/billie-holiday-lady-in-satin.listen: In I'm a Fool to Want You, listen to her hoarse, vulnerable voice against the full orchestra, and notice how she still keeps her own phrasing.

werk/billie-holiday-lady-sings-the-blues.text:
Lady Sings the Blues is Billie Holiday's sixth studio album and was released in December 1956, at the same time as her autobiography of the same title. It was her last record for Clef Records, since a year later that label was absorbed into Verve Records. The recordings come from sessions in 1954 and 1956. She is accompanied by, among others, the saxophonist Paul Quinichette, the trumpeter Charlie Shavers, the pianist Wynton Kelly and the guitarist Kenny Burrell.

The album also includes Strange Fruit, God Bless the Child and Good Morning Heartache. Her voice had, according to some, already declined in the 1950s, but the record is highly regarded: DownBeat gave it five out of five stars in 1956. On 10 November 1956 Holiday gave a sold-out concert at Carnegie Hall to celebrate the book.
werk/billie-holiday-lady-sings-the-blues.listen: Listen to the title song Lady Sings the Blues, written by Holiday herself with Herbie Nichols, and notice how she lets the phrases rest on a quiet accompaniment.

werk/billie-holiday-music-for-torching.text:
Music for Torching is the fourth studio album by the jazz singer Billie Holiday, a collection of torch songs. It was released in 1955 on Clef Records and was her first 12-inch LP for that label, after four 10-inch LPs. The music was recorded in two sessions in Los Angeles, two days apart. Those sessions also already yielded the material for the follow-up Velvet Mood.

Holiday sings accompanied by a small ensemble: Harry Edison on trumpet, Benny Carter on alto and tenor saxophone, Jimmy Rowles on piano, Barney Kessel on guitar, John Simmons on bass and Larry Bunker on drums. The repertoire consists of well-known songs by composers such as Cole Porter, Irving Berlin and Jerome Kern, including I Get a Kick Out of You and A Fine Romance.
werk/billie-holiday-music-for-torching.listen: Listen to I Get a Kick Out of You, at 5:42 the longest track on the record, and notice how her voice remains the centre within the small ensemble.

werk/billy-bragg-don-t-try-this-at-home.text:
Don't Try This at Home is Billy Bragg's sixth album and was released on 16 September 1991 on Go! Discs. The urban folk singer brought in remarkable guests. Johnny Marr of The Smiths co-wrote Sexuality and helped produce three tracks, and Michael Stipe and Peter Buck of R.E.M. play on You Woke Up My Neighbourhood.

The songs vary widely. Cindy of a Thousand Lives is about the photographer Cindy Sherman, God's Footballer about the footballer Peter Knowles, who quit to become a Jehovah's Witness. Tank Park Salute is about his father Dennis, who died when he was 18. Dolphins is a version of a song by Fred Neil. Reviews were positive: a critic at NME called it his best album, and Select wrote that he had freed himself from every pigeonhole.
werk/billy-bragg-don-t-try-this-at-home.listen: Listen to Tank Park Salute and follow the lyrics: notice how a very personal story about a father is told in just over three minutes.

werk/billy-bragg-life-s-a-riot-with-spy-.text:
Billy Bragg recorded the seven tracks of his debut from 2 to 4 February 1983 in the demo studio of Chappell Music, under the supervision of in-house producer Oliver Hitch. Everything went onto tape in one go, without mixing. Only he himself can be heard, with his electric guitar. The record played at 45 rpm and lasted almost sixteen minutes. The title refers to his nickname Spy vs Spy, which he used as a street musician, after the comic strip in Mad magazine.

The album was released on 1 July 1983 on Utility, a new label of Charisma. NME placed it third of the year at the end of 1983. Douglas Wolk wrote in Rolling Stone that it cut through the overblown pop music of 1983. In 2006 a reissue appeared with a second CD full of alternative versions.
werk/billy-bragg-life-s-a-riot-with-spy-.listen: In A New England, listen to the combination of voice and electric guitar without accompaniment. This love song later became a hit for Kirsty MacColl.

werk/billy-bragg-talking-with-the-taxman.text:
Talking With the Taxman About Poetry is Billy Bragg's third album and was released in September 1986. Whereas his earlier records consisted almost entirely of himself and a guitar, more musicians play here. John Porter and Kenny Jones produced. Guest appearances come from Kirsty MacColl and Johnny Marr. The title is also that of a poem by Vladimir Mayakovsky, which is printed in the liner notes. The sleeve carries the subtitle The Difficult Third Album.

The songs are political and personal. There Is Power in a Union is based on the song Battle Cry of Freedom. Levi Stubbs' Tears refers to the makers of the Motown hits and to the Four Tops, and became the biggest single. A reviewer at Rolling Stone thought the record as political as The Clash, as clever as Elvis Costello and as melodic as Ray Davies. Ira Robbins spoke of a great leap forward, with subtle accompaniment on the best songs.
werk/billy-bragg-talking-with-the-taxman.listen: In Levi Stubbs' Tears, listen to how the guitar and the horns support the lyrics without drowning them out.

werk/billy-bragg-workers-playtime.text:
Workers Playtime by Billy Bragg was released in 1988 on Go! Discs and was his fourth release but third full album. Joe Boyd and the guitarist Wiggy produced. Alongside him play, among others, Danny Thompson on double bass, Cara Tivey on piano and organ, B.J. Cole on pedal steel, and Michelle Shocked sings backing vocals. It is thus a full line-up.

The record reached eighteenth place on the English chart. The sleeve carries the subtitle Capitalism Is Killing Music, a joke on the campaign Home Taping Is Killing Music. A maximum price was also stated on it: the LP or cassette was not allowed to cost more than 4.99 pounds in England. In 2006 an expanded reissue appeared with demos and a track by Paul Weller.
werk/billy-bragg-workers-playtime.listen: In The Price I Pay, listen to which instruments can be heard alongside the guitar and the singer's voice.

werk/billy-cobham-crosswinds.text:
Crosswinds was the second album by the fusion drummer Billy Cobham and was released in 1974. In contrast to the earlier Spectrum, it contains mainly tracks at a medium and slow tempo. All of the music is by the bandleader himself. He also took the photograph on the sleeve himself; it runs across the spine from front to back.

The first side is filled by Spanish Moss, A Sound Portrait, a suite in four parts: Spanish Moss, Savannah the Serene, Storm and Flash Flood. Each part has its own soloists, including Garnett Brown, George Duke, Randy Brecker and John Abercrombie. The second side holds The Pleasant Pheasant, Heather and Crosswind. Heather later became the basis for 93 'til Infinity by Souls of Mischief.
werk/billy-cobham-crosswinds.listen: In Flash Flood, listen to the solos by Randy Brecker on trumpet and John Abercrombie on guitar.

werk/billy-cobham-spectrum.text:
Spectrum was the first solo album by the fusion drummer Billy Cobham. It was recorded at Electric Lady Studios, according to the bassist Leland Sklar in two or three days, almost always in the first or second take. Sklar and the pianist Jan Hammer remember that the music was recorded live and not touched up afterwards.

The guitarist Tommy Bolin, still little known at the time, plays on four tracks. In Taurian Matador he breaks a string during his solo and simply plays on. To the Women in My Life is a piece for solo piano, played by Hammer. Stratus later became the basis of a sample in Safe from Harm by Massive Attack. The first reviews were positive. Years later Scott Yanow called the album the drummer's best.
werk/billy-cobham-spectrum.listen: In Taurian Matador, listen to Tommy Bolin's guitar solo, around 1:45: can you hear what happens when his high E string breaks and he simply keeps playing?

werk/billy-cobham-total-eclipse.text:
Total Eclipse is the third album by the fusion drummer Billy Cobham and was released in 1974. All eight tracks are his own. He plays drums, timpani and, on two tracks, acoustic piano. His band includes the guitarist John Abercrombie, the brothers Michael and Randy Brecker on wind instruments, the trombonist Glenn Ferris, the keyboardist Milcho Leviev and the bassist Alex Blake. Ken Scott recorded the record.

The music is fusion, a mixture of jazz and rock. The opening track Solarization lasts more than eleven minutes and consists of five parts. In between are short pieces such as Lunarputians and The Moon Ain't Made of Green Cheese, which lasts less than a minute. The longest track is Sea of Tranquility, almost eleven minutes. The album reached number 6 on the Billboard jazz chart, number 12 on the R&B chart and number 36 on the pop chart.
werk/billy-cobham-total-eclipse.listen: Listen to Moon Germs and notice the first guitar solo, played by guest musician Cornell Dupree: how does that solo relate to the drumming beneath it?

werk/billy-eckstine-imagination.text:
Imagination is an album that Billy Eckstine recorded in 1958 and that was released on the EmArcy label. It contains well-known songs from the American songbook tradition, such as I Got a Right to Sing the Blues by Harold Arlen and Ted Koehler, Love Is Just around the Corner by Lewis Gensler and Leo Robin and the title song by Jimmy Van Heusen and Johnny Burke.

What a Little Moonlight Can Do, Lullaby of the Leaves, I Cover the Waterfront and I Wished on the Moon are also on the record, as is That's All by Alan Brandt and Bob Haymes. It is thus not an album of new material, but a compilation of existing songs by a variety of composers. The album was released in 1958, and the title song sits in the middle of the track list.
werk/billy-eckstine-imagination.listen: Listen to Imagination and pay particular attention to the voice: how does the singer sound in this quiet song, and what role does the accompaniment around him play?

werk/billy-joel-cold-spring-harbor.text:
Cold Spring Harbor is Billy Joel's debut album, released on 1 November 1971 by Family Productions. The title refers to a village on Long Island Sound, close to his home town, and the sleeve was photographed on Harbor Road. Tomorrow Is Today stems from his depression and hospitalisation the year before. Because of a mastering error the tracks ran slightly too fast, making his voice sound unnaturally high. He was furious when he heard the record. Producer Artie Ripp, owner of the masters, took the blame.

The record sold poorly and only received attention after Piano Man and later albums had become popular. In 1983 a remixed version at the correct speed was released on Columbia, without his involvement. He himself feels there is something wrong with it. She's Got a Way and Everybody Loves You Now he later released live on Songs in the Attic.
werk/billy-joel-cold-spring-harbor.listen: Listen to She's Got a Way and notice how piano and voice carry the song. It is a song he would go on to play often.

werk/billy-joel-piano-man.text:
Piano Man is Billy Joel's second studio album, released on 14 November 1973 on Columbia Records. It arose from legal problems with his previous label, Family Productions, and ultimately became his breakthrough. In the United Kingdom it was not released until April 1975, on CBS. The title song tells, in fictionalised form, of his experiences as a bar pianist in Los Angeles and reached number 25 on the American Hot 100. Travelin' Prayer and Worse Comes to Worst also made the chart.

Rolling Stone wrote that the record revealed a new seriousness and flexibility and compared the style with that of Elton John. Billboard saw a good opportunity for a quality artist on the radio. The album reached number 27 on the Billboard 200 and went gold in 1975. Even so, he received only 8,000 dollars in royalties from it.
werk/billy-joel-piano-man.listen: Listen to Piano Man and notice how the song tells a story about the people in a bar.

werk/billy-joel-streetlife-serenade.text:
After Piano Man, Billy Joel was under pressure to make a new album quickly. He toured clubs and theatres, supported big names such as the Beach Boys and had little time to write songs. He therefore recorded two instrumental tracks: Root Beer Rag and The Mexican Connection. The record came out in October 1974 and was recorded mainly with session musicians. Joel sings and plays piano and other keyboards, for the first time also a Moog.

Root Beer Rag became a fixture of his concerts, and Souvenir often closed the encores. Joel himself judged in 1993 that the record had interesting musical ideas but nothing to say lyrically. The album reached number 35 on the American chart and later sold more than a million copies.
werk/billy-joel-streetlife-serenade.listen: Listen to Root Beer Rag and notice how this instrumental track holds on to a melody and a rhythm even without vocals.

werk/billy-joel-the-stranger.text:
After the poorly selling Turnstiles, Columbia Records threatened to drop Billy Joel. He wanted to record his next record with his own touring band: drummer Liberty DeVitto, bassist Doug Stegmeyer and Richie Cannata on saxophone and organ. At first he thought of George Martin, but he eventually chose Phil Ramone as producer. The recording in the summer of 1977 took three weeks. Guitarists varied from track to track.

The album has nine tracks. The whistled main melody of the title track was whistled by Joel himself to Ramone, who thought it exactly right and let it stay. Movin' Out is about Anthony, a boy from Long Island with big dreams. Vienna came about after a visit to his father in Austria. Four singles reached the American Top 40, and Just the Way You Are won two Grammy Awards. The album became his commercial and artistic breakthrough.
werk/billy-joel-the-stranger.listen: In The Stranger, listen to the whistled melody. How does it change the mood of the song?

werk/billy-joel-turnstiles.text:
Turnstiles is partly a celebration of Joel's return to his home city of New York. The songs were first recorded in Colorado, with members of Elton John's band and producer James William Guercio. Joel was dissatisfied, took over the production and re-recorded the whole album in New York with his own touring band. For the first time that band played on a studio album of his.

Three tracks refer to New York, including New York State of Mind. The opening track Say Goodbye to Hollywood was inspired by Be My Baby by the Ronettes. In Prelude / Angry Young Man, Joel imitates the drums of Wipe Out with fast piano playing. According to AllMusic the success lies in the variety, from the swinging pop song to the barroom number. The album was released in May 1976.
werk/billy-joel-turnstiles.listen: Listen to Prelude / Angry Young Man and notice how Joel opens the piece with lightning-fast piano playing that sounds like drums.

werk/billy-preston-that-s-the-way-god-pl.text:
That's the Way God Planned It is Billy Preston's fourth studio album and was released in August 1969 on Apple Records. It came after his collaboration with the Beatles on the single Get Back and was produced by George Harrison. Harrison plays guitar, Moog and sitar. Eric Clapton, Keith Richards, Ginger Baker and Doris Troy also contribute. The title song became a hit in England as a single.

Record Collector wrote that the album presents the organist as a versatile, spiritually compelling singer-songwriter. David Fricke placed it in Rolling Stone among the five best Apple albums without the Beatles and called the rest of the record solid soul with church influences, with covers of Bob Dylan and W.C. Handy. According to him, the singer later had bigger hits, but never a better one than the title song.
werk/billy-preston-that-s-the-way-god-pl.listen: In That's the Way God Planned It, listen to the bass guitar, which is played by Keith Richards.

werk/billy-preston-the-most-exciting-org.text:
The Most Exciting Organ Ever is Billy Preston's second album. The record is entirely instrumental and was released in January 1965. The title says it all: the organ is central. Besides pieces by Preston himself there are versions of existing songs, such as If I Had a Hammer by Lee Hays and Pete Seeger and Slippin' and Slidin' by Richard Penniman and others.

The best-known track is Billy's Bag, which at the time was loved by British musicians and clubgoers. Preston later also recorded a live version of it, which is on his 1974 album Live European Tour. Extra tracks from the recording sessions for this record appeared on his next studio album.
werk/billy-preston-the-most-exciting-org.listen: Listen to Billy's Bag, the track that British musicians and clubgoers were crazy about at the time, and notice how the organ carries the whole piece without vocals.

werk/billy-preston-wildest-organ-in-town.text:
Wildest Organ in Town! was released in 1966 with arrangements by Sly Stone. Billy Preston plays organ in a mix of covers and original work. He reworks In the Midnight Hour by Wilson Pickett and Steve Cropper, Uptight by Stevie Wonder, A Hard Day's Night by Lennon and McCartney, Satisfaction by Mick Jagger and Keith Richards and I Got You by James Brown. There are also original tracks, such as Ain't Got No Time to Play, and three that he wrote together with Stone: Advice, It's Got to Happen and Free Funk.

The album reached number 118 on the Billboard 200. AllMusic wrote that his early talent as a flashy organ equivalent of Jimi Hendrix has largely been forgotten, and that it did not help that this record was unavailable for years.
werk/billy-preston-wildest-organ-in-town.listen: In A Hard Day's Night, listen to what the organ does with a familiar Beatles song.

werk/billy-ray-cyrus-home-at-last.text:
Home at Last is Billy Ray Cyrus's tenth studio album. It was released on 24 July 2007 and followed Wanna Be Your Joe from 2006. It is his first and only album for Walt Disney Records. The first single was Ready, Set, Don't Go. The song was released again in October 2007 as a duet with his daughter Miley, which they performed together on Dancing with the Stars. The duet version reached number 4 on the country chart.

Stand had first been recorded as a duet with Miley on the previous album, but was remixed for this album without her vocals. Home at Last reached number 3 on Top Country Albums and number 20 on the Billboard 200. It went gold and was his first album in thirteen years to be certified.
werk/billy-ray-cyrus-home-at-last.listen: Listen to Ready, Set, Don't Go, first the version with only his voice and then the duet with Miley Cyrus at the end, and hear what the second voice changes.

werk/billy-ray-cyrus-some-gave-all.text:
This debut album was released in 1992 on Mercury Records. That year it became the best-selling album in the United States, with more than nine million copies in the first year. It stood at the top of the Billboard 200 for seventeen weeks in a row, longer than any debut. Four singles reached the country charts: Could've Been Me, Wher'm I Gonna Live?, She's Not Cryin' Anymore and above all Achy Breaky Heart.

Achy Breaky Heart was the singer's breakthrough and reached the top in several countries. Thanks to the video, line dancing became a craze. The song had previously been recorded by the Marcy Brothers. The reviewer Robert Christgau felt that the singer overdid it and praised the self-mockery in three tracks. In 2006 Q magazine placed the album on a list of the worst albums. Even so, it is one of the best-selling debut albums ever.
werk/billy-ray-cyrus-some-gave-all.listen: Listen to Achy Breaky Heart: notice the self-mockery that Robert Christgau heard in it.

werk/billy-ray-cyrus-southern-rain.text:
Southern Rain is the sixth studio album by the American country singer Billy Ray Cyrus. He recorded it for Monument Records, after leaving Mercury in 1999, and released it in October 2000. He wrote the title song in his back garden during a rainstorm, while feeling gloomy about that departure. Many of the other tracks came to him through producers and the label. The opener You Won't Be Lonely Now was the first song he recorded.

We the People was intended as an event and features Waylon Jennings and John Anderson reciting the preamble of the United States Constitution. The George W. Bush campaign chose it as its theme song. Hey Elvis, a cover of Bryan Adams, is on the record as a bonus track. The album produced five singles on the country charts. Critical reception was mixed: AllMusic spoke of solid, average country songs.
werk/billy-ray-cyrus-southern-rain.listen: Listen to All I'm Thinking About Is You: notice the spoken verses, which Cyrus himself found different from anything he had recorded before.

werk/billy-ray-cyrus-the-other-side.text:
The Other Side is the eighth studio album by the country singer Billy Ray Cyrus, and the only one he recorded for Word Records. Its starting point is faith: Face of God opens the album and connects with a set of songs about hope and prayer, such as Did I Forget To Pray and Love Has No Walls. The album closes with Amazing Grace, in an arrangement by Cyrus and the guitarist Billy Joe Walker Jr.

Three singles were released: Always Sixteen, Face of God and I Need You Now. Face of God did best, reaching number 54 on the Hot Country Songs. Well-known songwriters contributed songs, including Richard Marx, who also sang along, and Bebo Norman. The studio musicians included Pat Buchanan, Brent Mason and Glenn Worf.
werk/billy-ray-cyrus-the-other-side.listen: Listen to Amazing Grace, the last track, and notice how sparse or full the accompaniment sounds around the voice.

werk/billy-squier-don-t-say-no.text:
Don't Say No is Billy Squier's second studio album, released on 13 April 1981. It became his greatest success. He produced it himself together with Reinhold Mack and played vocals, guitar and piano. Cary Sharaf plays the guitar solo on Lonely Is the Night.

The first single, The Stroke, did well on rock radio and also briefly made the British chart. In the Dark followed in the American top forty. Lonely Is the Night became one of his best-known songs, although it was not a proper single and had no video. The videos of this period show him on an arena stage and were regular guests on the new MTV. The album remained on the album chart for more than two years.
werk/billy-squier-don-t-say-no.listen: Listen to Lonely Is the Night and notice the guitar solo by Cary Sharaf. Note how it makes the song one of his best known.

werk/billy-squier-emotions-in-motion.text:
Emotions in Motion was released on 23 July 1982 as Billy Squier's third studio album. He produced it together with Reinhold Mack, as with its predecessor Don't Say No, and Mack was also known for Queen's The Game. Guitar and vocals came from Squier himself, and Bobby Chouinard played drums.

On the title song, Freddie Mercury and Roger Taylor of Queen sing backing vocals. The sleeve was made by Andy Warhol. Everybody Wants You was the biggest hit and spent six weeks at the top of the Mainstream Rock Tracks chart. Emotions in Motion and She's a Runner were also released as singles, and Learn How to Live received a lot of airplay. The album reached the top five of the Billboard chart and went gold and platinum within a few months.
werk/billy-squier-emotions-in-motion.listen: Listen to Emotions In Motion and try to hear where Freddie Mercury and Roger Taylor sing along in the background.

werk/billy-squier-signs-of-life.text:
Signs of Life is Billy Squier's fourth studio album. For the first time he did not work with Reinhold Mack, who had produced Don't Say No and Emotions in Motion. In his place came Jim Steinman, known as Meat Loaf's songwriter. The production was rich, with many synthesizers, and the songs sounded poppier. Larry Fast played synthesizers and Brian May added a guitar solo to (Another) 1984.

Rock Me Tonite became the singer's highest-charting pop single and reached the top of the Mainstream Rock chart. The accompanying video became notorious and is often seen as one of the reasons for his declining popularity. The record divided audiences and critics at the time, but is today regarded as one of his best works.
werk/billy-squier-signs-of-life.listen: Listen to (Another) 1984 and notice the guitar solo by Brian May.

werk/billy-squier-the-tale-of-the-tape.text:
Billy Squier made his first solo album in 1980, after having previously recorded two albums with the band Piper. He produced it together with Eddy Offord and himself played vocals, guitar and percussion. The guitarist Bruce Kulick and the keyboardist David Sancious took part, and the Woodstock Children's Chorus sang on the record.

The album was not a great success, but it spent three months on the American album chart and helped launch his solo career. No track reached the singles charts. The Big Beat, however, has often been sampled by hip hop artists since, including in Here We Go by Run-D.M.C. and in 99 Problems by Jay-Z. The song also had a video from before the MTV era. Billboard felt that the album fitted well alongside Journey and Styx.
werk/billy-squier-the-tale-of-the-tape.listen: Listen to The Big Beat and notice the beat. That is the part hip hop producers later sampled.

werk/bing-crosby-bing-sings-whilst-bregm.text:
Bing Sings Whilst Bregman Swings was Bing Crosby's sixth LP in 1956 and his first for Verve. It was a break in style: for the first time he recorded an album with an orchestra in the spirit of Frank Sinatra's Songs for Swingin' Lovers. Buddy Bregman came up with the plan, wrote the arrangements and conducted a group of Hollywood musicians. Crosby had never recorded many of the songs before, and his only condition was that he record at nine o'clock in the morning, because his voice was at its best then.

Variety and Billboard were enthusiastic; Time felt that he only sounded old when he tried to swing too high. Producer Ken Barnes praised the choice of songs, such as They All Laughed and Have You Met Miss Jones?, but criticised Bregman's heavy brass arrangements.
werk/bing-crosby-bing-sings-whilst-bregm.listen: In They All Laughed, listen to Crosby's casual singing set against the orchestra.

werk/bing-crosby-when-irish-eyes-are-smi.text:
When Irish Eyes Are Smiling is an album by Bing Crosby of songs with an Irish theme, released by Decca as a 10-inch LP. Some of the tracks had previously appeared on a set of three singles. Later a 12-inch version with the same title and a different selection of tracks was released.

Crosby had Irish ancestors on his mother's side and heard traditional Irish songs as a child. His first Irish recording was Did Your Mother Come from Ireland? in 1940, and from then on Irish songs remained a fixed part of his repertoire. The success of an earlier Irish album led Decca to put together another album in the same vein. It contained two new songs, St. Patrick's Day Parade and With My Shillelagh Under My Arm. Billboard praised the first as a new song of superior quality and found the second somewhat less strong.
werk/bing-crosby-when-irish-eyes-are-smi.listen: Listen to St. Patrick's Day Parade and notice how the singer gives his voice an Irish accent.

werk/bjork-debut.text:
After the break-up of the Sugarcubes, Björk moved to London. The guitar rock of her previous group felt outdated, and the city's club culture showed her that house music was modern pop music. Many songs she had written years earlier, such as Human Behaviour. She first worked with Graham Massey of 808 State and with jazz musicians, but ultimately chose the producer Nellee Hooper. By early 1993 Debut was finished.

The album mixes electronic pop, house, jazz and trip hop. It sounds different from the grunge and Britpop of the time. On Aeroplane and The Anchor Song saxophonists can be heard, led by Oliver Lake, and Like Someone in Love is a jazz standard. British critics were full of praise, American reviews mixed. The album sold better than expected and remained her best-selling record in the United States.
werk/bjork-debut.listen: Listen to The Anchor Song and notice the saxophones that carry the song. Can you hear how the voice is placed among those horns?

werk/bjork-drawing-restraint-9.text:
Björk made this music for Drawing Restraint 9, the film by Matthew Barney in which she also appears. For the composition she travelled to Japan to study old Japanese music. Several pieces are built on the sound of the shō, a Japanese wind instrument with sixteen reeds, played by Mayumi Miyata. Zeena Parkins, who had already played on Vespertine, provides harp. On the opening track Will Oldham sings a letter from a Japanese fisherman to General MacArthur.

She herself sings on only three tracks. Storm is made from a song that she played on tour in 2003 and that, with help from Leila, she turned into a loop. The album was released in July 2005 and is her second soundtrack.
werk/bjork-drawing-restraint-9.listen: Listen to Storm. Notice the singing voice and how it repeats and builds.

werk/bjork-homogenic.text:
After a long tour for Post, Björk returned to her home in London, needing to write new songs as a form of therapy. A media circus around her stalker disrupted the sessions, and she withdrew to Spain, to the studio of her drummer Trevor Morais in Málaga. There she recorded most of the album, with Mark Bell, Guy Sigsworth, Howie B and Markus Dravs, among others, as producers.

Homogenic is a tribute to Iceland. Electronic beats form the rhythm, the heartbeat-like part, and the Icelandic String Octet provides the strings. Producer Dravs described the desired sound as raw volcanoes with soft moss over them. Her singing ranges from screaming to the singing and speaking style of Icelandic choirmen, as in Unravel. The album received broad praise and has since appeared on many lists of the best records of all time.
werk/bjork-homogenic.listen: Listen to Unravel. Notice how her voice moves between speaking and singing, and how little is happening beneath the vocals.

werk/bjork-medulla.text:
Medúlla is Björk's fifth studio album and was released in August 2004. After the electronic Vespertine she wanted to make a record consisting almost entirely of human voices. She had had that desire since her teenage years. The title comes from the Latin word for marrow. She began in 2002, still under the working title The Lake Album. She added her own drums to demos while eight months pregnant and then switched the instruments off, because she liked the result.

Guest singers included the Inuit throat singer Tanya Tagaq, Robert Wyatt and Mike Patton of Faith No More. Choirs from London and Iceland also took part. Beatboxers such as Rahzel and Dokaka provide the rhythms. Two singles were released from the record, Who Is It and Triumph of a Heart. She sang Oceania at the opening of the 2004 Olympic Games. Critical reception was full of praise, although some found the album confusing. It received two Grammy nominations.
werk/bjork-medulla.listen: Listen to Who Is It and try to hear which sounds and rhythms come from human voices.

werk/bjork-post.text:
After Debut, Björk lived in London and wanted to make a tougher, more outward-looking album. In late 1994 she began at Compass Point Studios in the Bahamas, where she stood in the sea at sunset to record vocals. She produced it herself, together with Nellee Hooper, Graham Massey and Tricky, among others. Army of Me and The Modern Things she had already written earlier. Back in London she tinkered on for months and re-recorded tracks, until real instruments brought the album to life.

The result is a colourful mixture of techno, trip hop, house, jazz and experimental music. Isobel has strings on breakbeats, It's Oh So Quiet is a big band number and Headphones closes quietly with studio tricks meant for headphones. Post was released in June 1995 and reached second place in the United Kingdom. Critics praised the ambition and found the record timeless.
werk/bjork-post.listen: Listen to Isobel and notice the interplay of the orchestral strings and the fast breakbeats beneath them. Does that suit a fairy tale about a woman from the forest?

werk/bjork-selmasongs.text:
In 2000 the soundtrack of the film Dancer in the Dark was released, in which Björk played the lead role. She had first been asked only to write the music, but director Lars von Trier persuaded her to play Selma as well, a Czech immigrant who is slowly going blind and works in a factory. She made the music partly with sounds she recorded on the film set, such as factory machines and trains.

That yields a mixture of classical arrangements, techno rhythms and musical melodies. Cvalda begins with industrial sounds that turn into a shuffling rhythm. I've Seen It All rests on a rhythmic loop of train sounds, and Thom Yorke sings the part of Peter Stormare from the film there. That song received an Oscar nomination. Some lyrics were adapted for the album, and a few songs from the film are missing. Reviews were mostly favourable.
werk/bjork-selmasongs.listen: In Cvalda, listen to the factory sounds with which the song begins. Notice how a rhythm grows out of them.

werk/bjork-vespertine.text:
Vespertine is Björk's fourth studio album, released in August 2001. After the loud Homogenic she wanted to make a record of small, intricate electronic music with a domestic feel. The first working title was Domestika. She began it while shooting the film Dancer in the Dark, and her new relationship with Matthew Barney made the lyrics more intimate. Producers included Opiate, Console and the duo Matmos, and the harpist Zeena Parkins contributed.

The arrangements use delicate instruments such as harp, celesta, clavichord, strings and specially made music boxes. Together with Matmos she made microbeats from everyday sounds, such as the shuffling of cards and the cracking of ice. Three singles were released from Vespertine: Hidden Place, Pagan Poetry and Cocoon. The videos for the last two were rejected by MTV. Critics were unanimous in their praise and called the record erotic, intimate and experimental. It appeared on many lists of the best albums of 2001 and of the decade.
werk/bjork-vespertine.listen: Listen to Cocoon and notice how soft and close everything sounds, as if the music were being made in a room around you.

werk/bjork-vulnicura.text:
After the tour for Biophilia, Björk began a new album about the time before and after her break-up with the artist Matthew Barney and about the recovery afterwards. The title is Latin and means healing of wounds. She produced it with the Venezuelan Arca and with The Haxan Cloak. To keep her mind occupied she wrote the string arrangements for fifteen strings. Arca joined late in the process: they worked side by side for weeks, and according to her that was the most fun she had ever had making music, with the most tragic subject.

The sound consists mainly of strings and electronic beats, a return to the direction of Homogenic from 1997. The album leaked two months early and therefore appeared digitally on 20 January 2015. There were no singles, but there was a series of innovative videos. Critics called it one of her most honest and personal records. It was nominated for a Grammy.
werk/bjork-vulnicura.listen: Listen to Atom Dance and notice how the strings and the electronic beats together accompany Björk's voice.

werk/bl-f-zoutelande.text: In 2017 BLØF had a big hit with Zoutelande, a duet with the Flemish singer Geike Arnaert about a beach in Zeeland. The song was a Dutch adaptation of a German song. It spent weeks at number one and for years was one of the most streamed Dutch-language songs. The little village of Zoutelande suddenly received many extra tourists.
werk/bl-f-zoutelande.listen: Hear how the two voices alternate, the Zeelandic and the Flemish, over a calm, summery beat.

werk/black-flag-damaged.text:
Damaged was the debut album of the hardcore punk band and was released in November 1981 on SST Records. Earlier attempts to record an album had failed with three different singers. Now the twenty-year-old Henry Rollins sang, who had only been in the band for a few weeks. The group first recorded the instruments, after which Rollins put his vocals over the top. Recording took place at Unicorn Studios in West Hollywood. The last track, Damaged I, was his first writing credit.

As well as the lyrics, the record company stood in the way: MCA refused to distribute the record because its boss considered it an anti-parent record. A lawsuit followed that kept the band occupied for almost two years. Critics and the public largely ignored the album on release. It was later recognised as one of the most influential punk records ever, and the sleeve, with Rollins's fist through a mirror, became famous.
werk/black-flag-damaged.listen: Listen to TV Party and notice the singing of the whole band in the chorus. Also hear how the joke in the song fits the fast tempo of the record.

werk/black-sabbath-heaven-and-hell.text:
In 1979 Black Sabbath was in disarray. Ozzy Osbourne had left and the new singer Ronnie James Dio met the guitarist Tony Iommi through Sharon Arden. On their first day together they finished Children of the Sea, a song that Iommi had left lying. The line-up remained shaky: drummer Bill Ward was struggling with personal problems and bassist Geezer Butler was going through a divorce. Dio suggested Martin Birch as producer, the first outsider behind the controls since Master of Reality. Recording took place at Criteria Studios in Miami and Studios Ferber in Paris.

Iommi noticed that Dio sang differently from Osbourne. Whereas Osbourne followed the melody of the riff, Dio sang across it, which opened up new possibilities for Iommi. The album was released on 18 April 1980 and was a great success, especially in America, where it went platinum. It was the group's ninth record and the first with Dio.
werk/black-sabbath-heaven-and-hell.listen: Listen to Heaven and Hell and notice how Dio's vocal rides over the riff instead of following it.

werk/black-sabbath-master-of-reality.text:
Black Sabbath was already a successful band in 1971, despite the criticism of their music. After the debut and Paranoid, the group recorded the third album at Island Studios in London, from February to April. Rodger Bain produced, for the last time. There was more time than before and the band dared to experiment: Tony Iommi added classical guitar parts and Bill Ward tried overdubs.

The sound comes from tuning down. Iommi tuned his guitar a tone and a half lower, partly because, after an accident to his fingertips, he was in pain when playing, and Geezer Butler did the same with his bass. The result was bigger, heavier and drier, audible in Children of the Grave, Lord of This World and Into the Void. Sweet Leaf is about the weed the band smoked. Critics were negative, but the album is now regarded as one of the best heavy metal records.
werk/black-sabbath-master-of-reality.listen: Listen to Children of the Grave and notice the heavy, low guitar riff and the galloping rhythm beneath it.

werk/black-sabbath-mob-rules.text:
Mob Rules is Black Sabbath's tenth studio album and came out on 4 November 1981. It followed Heaven and Hell and brought singer Ronnie James Dio for the second time and drummer Vinny Appice for the first time on a record by the band. Appice had replaced Bill Ward halfway through the Heaven and Hell tour. The first new recording was The Mob Rules for the film Heavy Metal. The band had bought a studio of their own, but could not get a good guitar sound there and ultimately recorded the album at Record Plant in Los Angeles. Martin Birch produced, for the last time.

Reviews were mixed at first. AllMusic called the album underrated and praised the spirited mix, although the sequence closely resembles that of Heaven and Hell. Later it was mostly judged favourably. In England it reached the top twenty, with two singles: The Mob Rules and Turn Up the Night.
werk/black-sabbath-mob-rules.listen: In The Sign of the Southern Cross, listen to Geezer Butler's bass effects; he names this his favourite song on the album.

werk/black-sabbath-paranoid.text:
After the success of the debut, Black Sabbath went back into the studio in June 1970, four months later, with producer Rodger Bain. The recordings at Regent Sound and Island Studios in London were finished in a few days. Many tracks had arisen from jam sessions on stage, including during a six-week stay at a club in Zürich. The title track came about as an afterthought: there were too few songs, and Tony Iommi played the guitar riff in some twenty minutes. It became a single and reached fourth place in the United Kingdom.

War Pigs was first meant to be called Walpurgis, but Geezer Butler's lyrics target warmongers. On Planet Caravan, Ozzy Osbourne sings through a Leslie speaker. The album is regarded as one of the most influential metal albums. In 2017 Rolling Stone placed it first on its list of the best metal albums.
werk/black-sabbath-paranoid.listen: Listen to Planet Caravan and notice the vocals, which sound through a Leslie speaker and so very different from elsewhere on the album.

werk/black-sabbath-sabotage.text:
Sabotage came about in a difficult time. Black Sabbath began the sixth album in February 1975 at Morgan Studios in London, while the band was being sued by former manager Patrick Meehan. That is where the title comes from. Drummer Bill Ward said it was probably the only album made with lawyers in the studio. Guitarist Tony Iommi produced together with Mike Butcher.

The record combines heavy tracks with experiments. Hole in the Sky opens, Symptom of the Universe begins acoustically and turns into fast playing with a jam at the end, and on Supertzar the English Chamber Choir sings. On The Writ, Ozzy Osbourne wrote the lyrics himself. The first reviews were positive. The album was released on 28 July 1975 and is still regarded as a classic, although it became the band's first without platinum in the United States.
werk/black-sabbath-sabotage.listen: In Symptom of the Universe, listen to the transition from the acoustic beginning to the fast section, and to the jam at the end.

werk/black-sabbath-technical-ecstasy.text:
After the protracted legal battles surrounding Sabotage in 1975, Black Sabbath chose Criteria Studios in Miami. The band wanted to distance themselves from the darkness of the earlier records. Nobody wanted to take on the production, so it was left to guitarist Tony Iommi. Singer Ozzy Osbourne was already thinking of leaving, and in the age of rising punk the group felt unsure about its direction. Technical Ecstasy, released in October 1976, sounds more varied and complex than its predecessors, with plenty of keyboards and studio effects. The funky All Moving Parts (Stand Still) and the pop ballad It's Alright show this well. On the latter, drummer Bill Ward sings: for the first time it was not Osbourne singing a song by the band.

The reception was mixed. Many critics found it a confused album, and band members too later saw it as the beginning of the end. Even so, some praise the opener Back Street Kids and Dirty Women.
werk/black-sabbath-technical-ecstasy.listen: Listen to It's Alright and notice the singer: this is drummer Bill Ward, not Ozzy Osbourne, and the song sounds like a melodic pop ballad.

werk/black-sabbath-vol-4.text:
Despite the success of three albums, Black Sabbath struggled with problems in 1972, mainly because of drug use. For this album the band worked in America, in a rented house in Bel Air. It was the first record without producer Rodger Bain. Guitarist Tony Iommi did most of the production work, while manager Patrick Meehan was credited as co-producer. The recording was plagued by cocaine. The working title was Snowblind, but Vertigo did not want such a clear reference to drugs.

The music remains crushingly heavy, in Tomorrow's Dream, Cornucopia and Supernaut among others, but also goes in new directions. Changes is experimental and Laguna Sunrise is a neoclassical instrumental piece, conceived after a night of carousing on the beach. The music press remained critical, but the album was a great commercial success: number 5 in England and number 13 in America. It is now regarded as one of the band's best albums.
werk/black-sabbath-vol-4.listen: In Laguna Sunrise, listen to how the band here plays not heavy riffs but a calm, neoclassical instrumental piece.
